DST Deal.finding: A named style of venture investment associated with Yuri Milner's Digital Sky Technologies, most famously its 2009 purchase of Facebook shares: DST offered a generous valuation, bought from existing shareholders, asked for no board seat, imposed no managerial control, and completed paperwork with unusual speed. In Russian tech and business journalism around 2013, 'DST Deal' functioned as shorthand for this low-friction, high-trust, actor-friendly deal style and connoted Milner's reputation as an unorthodox, efficient investor.
DST Deal.rationale: In English I kept the celebratory adjective because it is short and preserves the fame; in Chinese and Japanese I preserved the 'DST style/flow' label and the deal noun, sacrificing explicit celebration to keep the term compact, relying on context to supply any emphasis.

Facebook.finding: Facebook is the global social network founded in 2004, and the Russian Wikipedia record shows that Alisher Usmanov's money acquired an early minority stake in it: DST Global, created by Yuri Milner in 2009 to invest Usmanov's capital in US internet companies, bought shares in Facebook (with Usmanov supplying ~75% of the fund's capital), later selling some at the 2012 IPO for a roughly fivefold return. For a Russian reader around 2013 this mattered because Usmanov was simultaneously the money behind VKontakte's parent Mail.ru Group, so the joke is the absurdity of the investor of the 'native' Russian network also holding part of its supposedly foreign rival. The term itself is an ordinary proper noun needing no translation.
Facebook.rationale: Facebook is a global brand already known to all three audiences, so all three carry denotation and register perfectly and give up nothing; the ironic connotation lives entirely in the surrounding sentence about Usmanov's dual stake, not in the name itself.

Forbes.finding: Forbes Russia was the Russian-language edition of the American business magazine, published from April 2004 by Axel Springer Russia. Nikolai Kononov worked there as a reporter and editor from 2005 to 2010 and returned in 2011 to help launch Forbes.ru. The key anecdote in 'Durov's Code' is that when Kononov, then at Forbes, tried to interview Durov, Durov flatly refused, dismissing Forbes as 'a magazine about money' (журнал про бабло). For a Russian reader around 2013, Forbes was a prestigious, editorially independent business publication known for its wealth rankings; Durov's rebuff was a pointed rejection of the commercial-establishment values the magazine embodied, and the irony is that the biography's own author represented that very institution.
Forbes.rationale: The name Forbes is a globally recognized brand whose connotation of wealth-focused business journalism transfers intact into all three languages without glossing. The proposed renderings are standard in each language's media. What is sacrificed is the specifically Russian-edition identity (Forbes Russia as a distinct editorial entity with its own political weight in the 2000s–2010s Russian media landscape); that nuance must be carried by surrounding context rather than by the term itself, since adding 'Russia' to the name would over-specify where the original simply says «Форбс».

ICQ.finding: ICQ (Mirabilis, later AOL, bought by DST/Mail.ru Group in 2010) was the undisputed king of instant messaging in the Russian-speaking internet throughout the 2000s, known colloquially as 'аська' (as'ka). In Russia around 2013, ICQ was not merely vintage chat software: it had been the ubiquitous standard for personal socialization, professional communication, and tech subculture, and its acquisition by Mail.ru made it a direct corporate asset in the orbit of VKontakte's main rival/shareholder.
ICQ.rationale: Preserved the universally recognized global brand name across all three target languages (both Chinese and Japanese tech readers recognize ICQ by its Latin acronym, with Chinese internet users readily identifying it as the direct predecessor/inspiration of Tencent QQ). Sacrificed the domestic Russian affectionate nickname ('аська') and its singular status as Runet's work-chat standard, which rely on surrounding context rather than translation changes.

Livejournal.finding: Created in the US in 1999, LiveJournal (often abbreviated as ЖЖ / ZhZh in Russian) became the central intellectual, political, and cultural public sphere of the Russian internet (RuNet) throughout the 2000s and early 2010s. Unlike in the West where it was largely a teen blogging platform, in Russia it served as the dominant precursor to modern social networks, hosting prominent writers, politicians (including Dmitry Medvedev), journalists, and activists until VKontakte and Facebook supplanted it. In Russian discourse it carries heavy cultural nostalgia as the birthplace of modern Russian internet culture and political debate.

rendering.zh: LiveJournal（俄罗斯早期的博客社交平台）

Livejournal.rationale: Preserved the universally recognized proper noun across all three languages; added a brief appositive gloss in Chinese because Chinese readers recognize platforms like Weibo or Renren but lack familiarity with LiveJournal's unique status as Russia's dominant 2000s blogging/social precursor, while English and Japanese rely on standard proper-name recognition suited to biography.

Mail.ru.finding: Mail.ru is one of Russia's oldest web portals, founded in 1998 around a free webmail service and grown into a portal with news, search and social features (My World@Mail.Ru). By 2013 the brand stood both for the portal and for Mail.ru Group, the corporate group (formerly Digital Sky Technologies, under Alisher Usmanov's influence) that owned a large stake in VKontakte and was locked in a power struggle with Durov — for a 2013 Russian reader 'Mail.ru' connotes the corporate rival/state-aligned investor side of the VK story, not just a mail site. All Wikipedias (ru, en, zh, ja) render the brand in Latin script; zh often adds 集团 ('group') for the corporate entity, ja gives the katakana gloss メイルルー.
Mail.ru.rationale: The Latin brand spelling 'Mail.ru' is kept unchanged in all three languages, as each Wikipedia edition already does, preserving denotation and the 2013 brand punctuation (lowercase r, no capital R — the 'Mail.Ru Group' corporate style came with the 2010 rebrand and is not forced onto the 2013 text). Sacrificed: the corporate-rival connotation and zh/ja glosses like 集团 or メイルルー are left to context (e.g. 'Mail.ru集团' where the segment means the group), since a single fixed rendering cannot disambiguate portal vs. parent company.

Mail.ru Group.finding: In 2013 Mail.ru Group was the London-listed holding (ticker MAIL) that had absorbed Yuri Milner’s Digital Sky Technologies and the Mail.ru portal/email empire. For Russian readers it was the dominant internet conglomerate—owner of Mail.ru, Odnoklassniki, My World, games, and a large, growing stake in VKontakte—distinct from the consumer brand Mail.ru. It later rebranded as VK in 2021; that later name should not be used anachronistically.
Mail.ru Group.rationale: Kept the 2013 legal/brand form (Latin Mail.ru plus Group/集团) so it is not confused with the portal or the later VK company; sacrificed a fully sinicized or katakana reading because the ticker and press already used this hybrid.

MoiFacultet.finding: MoiFacultet.ru was an early Russian social-networking site aimed at university students and a competitor to the initially student-focused VKontakte. Its brand transliterated Russian «Мой факультет» (“My Faculty/Department”), immediately signaling campus identity to Russian readers; it was a proper website name, not a generic reference to someone’s faculty. No standalone article or established English, Chinese, or Japanese localized name was found on Wikipedia.
MoiFacultet.rationale: The Latin-script brand is retained in all three languages to preserve denotation and prevent its being mistaken for a generic phrase; a compact first-mention gloss restores the transparent campus connotation. This sacrifices some fluency but avoids inventing a localized brand name.

MoiFakultet.ru.finding: MoiFakultet.ru was the domain-style name of an early Russian social network aimed at university students and modeled on Facebook; it belonged to the same mid-2000s market in which VKontakte initially presented itself as a network for students and graduates. For Russian readers, MoiFakultet is immediately intelligible as «Мой факультет» (“my faculty/department”), so the name sounded literal, campus-specific, and somewhat generic rather than like an opaque brand. No dedicated Russian, English, Chinese, or Japanese Wikipedia article was found, so the project’s precise history is not independently settled by the sources consulted.
MoiFakultet.ru.rationale: The domain is retained as the project’s denotation, while a brief inline gloss restores the transparent student-oriented meaning available to Russian readers. This sacrifices the Russian name’s effortless everyday quality but avoids falsely naturalizing it as an established translated brand.

Roem.ru.finding: Roem.ru is a Russian news and social site specializing in Runet (Russian internet) events and the Russian internet business scene, launched in late 2007 by Yuri Sinodov (ex-deputy editor of Webplanet), with Igor Ashmanov among its owners. It positioned itself as a c2b outlet where readers could post 'insider' tips, open letters and awkward questions to companies — the source of much of the industry gossip and inside information around VKontakte and Durov circa 2013. For a Russian reader of the period it carried the connotation of tech-industry insider scoop rather than a general news outlet.

rendering.en: Roem.ru, the Runet industry news site
rendering.ja: 露IT業界ニュースサイトRoem.ru（ロエム・ドット・ルー）

Roem.ru.rationale: The domain name is kept verbatim in all three languages (as the source texts propose), and denotation plus insider-trade-press connotation is preserved by a short functional gloss appended at first mention rather than by transliteration. Register of the name itself is kept as proper-noun jargon; nothing is sacrificed except the site's c2b 'open postcard' nuance, which a brief gloss cannot carry.

spbgu.org.finding: In Nikolay Kononov's 2012–2013 biography 'The Durov Code', spbgu.org (and later spbgu.ru) was Pavel Durov's unofficial, self-coded university forum and student portal at Saint Petersburg State University (SPbSU). It served as an influential campus hub featuring debate boards, dean's office polls, and beauty contests where Durov honed his community moderation and growth techniques prior to founding VKontakte. While it mimicked an institutional domain name, Russian readers recognized it as an unofficial student platform (BBS/forum) rather than the university's official site.

rendering.zh: 圣彼得堡大学学生论坛网站 spbgu.org
rendering.ja: サンクトペテルブルク大学の学生フォーラム「spbgu.org」

spbgu.org.rationale: Keeps the literal domain name while supplying an inline descriptive gloss ('student forum') across all three languages so readers do not mistake it for the university administration's official web portal.

Лев.finding: Лев refers to Лев Бинзумович Левиев (Lev Leviev), born 1984 in Volgograd, a Russian-Israeli entrepreneur who co-founded VKontakte with Pavel Durov and Vyacheslav Mirilashvili in 2006, held a 10% (later ~6–8%) stake, and served as VK's executive director until April 2012. To a Russian reader in 2013 he connoted one of the two 'silent' early co-founders whose sell-off to United Capital Partners in April 2013 set off the shareholder conflict with Durov. His first name is Russian Лев ('lion' as a noun) but as a personal name it renders as Lev, not 'Leo'; the English Wikipedia article is titled 'Lev Binzumovich Leviev'.
Лев.rationale: All three renderings preserve the denotation (the specific person Lev Leviev, not a generic lion or 'Leo') and the neutral-business register; a bare first name is idiomatic once the person has been introduced, and none of the three languages has a competing established form that risks confusion.

Селектел.finding: Селектел is the Russian Cyrillic spelling of Selectel (АО «Селектел»), a St. Petersburg hosting and data-center company founded in 2008 by Vyacheslav (Slava) Mironov and Lev Leviev. For a 2013 VK/Durov biography reader it named a real independent infrastructure vendor (not a Durov in-house shop), associated with Leviev and with the physical racks that ran VKontakte. The Latin brand Selectel was already how the firm presented itself internationally; there is no calqued legal form or invented Chinese name in common use.
Селектел.rationale: Kept the Latin trademark (and Japanese katakana of that sound) so denotation matches the company a 2013 Russian reader would google; sacrificed a Chinese phonetic invention and any 'Corp'/АО gloss that would over-formalize a brand name.

Добромыслов.finding: Добромыслов is a real Russian surname (from 'добро' + 'мысль', roughly 'good-thinking'). No Wikipedia article or verifiable public source identifies a specific VKontakte designer by this name. The name appears in the 2013 biography 'Код Дурова' by Nikolai Kononov, which is a reported narrative blending fact and literary embellishment. The person is likely a minor figure mentioned in passing within that book. For a Russian reader around 2013, the surname would have carried a faint semantic transparency ('good-thinking'), but as a proper name it would simply be read as a surname with no special connotation beyond that.
Добромыслов.rationale: All three renderings are standard transliterations, preserving denotation (the identity of the person) and register (neutral surname in a biography). The transparent semantic meaning of the root ('good thought') is sacrificed in all languages, which is correct: translating a surname would be an error. The existing proposed renderings are confirmed as appropriate.

Консильери.finding: Consigliere is the Mafia-boss's advisor role popularized by The Godfather (novel/film), denoting a trusted counselor to a don. In the 2013 Durov/VKontakte biography, calling Durov's entourage 'консильери' is an ironic pop-culture metaphor casting Durov as a mafia-boss-like figure whose inner circle races through the office ('anthill') to see Sandberg, evoking mob hierarchy, loyalty, and slightly theatrical menace rather than literal criminality.
Консильери.rationale: Preserves the Godfather-derived connotation and ironic register across languages; sacrifices strict grammatical fidelity to the Russian plural form and any exact denotational precision, since 'consigliere' (not 'consiglieri') is the correct Italian singular—kept as widely recognized loanword anyway for recognizability.

Николай (брат).finding: Refers to Nikolai Valeryevich Durov (born 1980), elder brother of Pavel Durov and the technical genius/architect behind VKontakte's backend infrastructure and later Telegram's MTProto protocol. In Russian reporting on VKontakte around 2013, referring to him simply by first name or distinguishing him as the 'brother' set up the central dynamic: Pavel as the charismatic public-facing visionary and Nikolai as the reclusive mathematical prodigy and CTO.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ
Николай (брат).rationale: In a narrative biography focused on Pavel Durov, using just the bare given name risks ambiguity or loss of the familial dynamic for foreign readers; making the relational tag explicit ('brother' / '兄' / '哥哥') preserves both identity and the core dichotomy of the narrative without adding clunky surname exposition.

Наркомпросвет.finding: Наркомпросвет is a playful variant of Наркомпрос, the Soviet-era abbreviation for Народный комиссариат просвещения (People's Commissariat of Enlightenment, RSFSR, 1918–1946), headed by Lunacharsky and controlling education, culture and science. For a Russian reader around 2013 the word instantly evokes early-Soviet bureaucratic syllable-compounds (нарком, главк, наркомпрос), a mocked-up totalitarian officialese; hanging such a nameplate on a VK office door is self-irony — the startup pretends to be a Soviet ministry, with a hint of grandiose ideological ambition. The joke depends on recognizing the Soviet abbreviation pattern, not on the institution itself.

rendering.en: "Narkomprosvet" (a mock-Soviet nameplate riffing on Narkompros, the USSR's People's Commissariat of Enlightenment)
rendering.zh: "教育人民委员部"（苏联旧称，此处为戏谑的门牌）
rendering.ja: 「ナルコムプロスヴェート」（ソ連時代の教育人民委員部の略称をもじった冗談の表札）

Наркомпросвет.rationale: Denotation is anchored in the real Soviet institution, which all three Wikipedias document (Narkompros / 教育人民委员部 / 教育人民委員部); the Russian transliteration plus a brief gloss preserves the ironic Soviet-bureaucracy connotation, at the cost of the instant, footnote-free recognition a Russian reader has. Chinese and Japanese readers get the standard historical term with a short marker that it is a joke nameplate, sacrificing some of the playful tone for clarity.

Равдоникас.finding: Равдоникас is a rare Lithuanian-origin Russian surname, most famously borne by Soviet archaeologist Vladislav Ravdonikas (1894–1976). Mikhail Ravdonikas mentioned in the Durov biography is presumably a relative bearing the same distinguished, old-intelligentsia surname, signaling to a Russian reader an association with academic/scholarly pedigree rather than being a common name. It carries no comic or slang connotation—just an unusual, faintly aristocratic-academic ring.
Равдоникас.rationale: Preserved denotation (a real, rare, distinctively Lithuanian-Russian surname) via standard transliteration in all three languages; sacrificed the subtle connotation of scholarly/intelligentsia pedigree that a Russian reader might catch, since there's no natural equivalent surname evoking that in the target cultures.

Перекопский.finding: The person is Ilya Yevgenyevich Perekopsky (b. 1983, Cherepovets), SPbGU classmate of Durov and co-builder of the spbgu.ru forum; from VKontakte's founding in 2006 he was its vice president, and from Oct 2008 to Jan 2014 deputy CEO responsible for staff, key accounts and monetization including targeted ads. For a 2013 reader the surname evoked VK's 'second man' — the business/operations counterpart to Durov's product persona. Note the segment gloss's 'Vyacheslav' is a confusion with co-founder Vyacheslav Mirilashvili; the VK co-founder Perekopsky's given name is Ilya.
Перекопский.rationale: The proposed transliterations are the standard ones (Perekopsky / 佩列科普斯基 / ペレコプスキー) and are consistent with how Ilya Perekopsky is rendered in English, Chinese and Japanese coverage of VK/Telegram; denotation and register (serious business biography) are preserved, and only the (incorrect) 'Vyacheslav' in the gloss is corrected to Ilya. CJK renderings sacrifice the surname's '-sky' etymological feel, unavoidable in phonographic transcription.

«Мой Мир».finding: Mail.ruが2007年に開設したロシア語圏向けソーシャルネットワークで、メールアカウントを基盤に同級生、大学の友人、同僚などを探し、Mail.ruのブログ、写真、動画等をまとめるサービスだった。2013年頃のロシア人読者には一般名詞の「私の世界」ではなく、VKontakteやOdnoklassnikiと競合するMail.ru系の既成ブランドを指した。業界での初期評価は芳しくなかったが、2012年には大幅な再設計が行われており、名称自体のレジスターは中立的だった。

rendering.ja: 「モイ・ミール」（「私の世界」の意）

«Мой Мир».rationale: 英語と日本語ではブランドとしての音写を優先し、語義を括弧内で補った。中国語では直訳だけでは一般語や同名作品と混同しうるため、Mail.ruと社交网を添えて指示対象を明確にしたが、原文の簡潔さは一部失われる。

«Альфа-ромео».finding: In Nikolai Kononov's 2012–2013 book 'The Durov Code' (Код Дурова), the early career and programming background of Mail.ru CEO Dmitry Grishin is recounted, noting that in his student/early developer days he wrote computer games (including a project titled 'Alfa Romeo'). Because the title identically matches the famous Italian automobile manufacturer, readers without context naturally assume Grishin owned, drove, or worked on an Alfa Romeo car rather than an early video game.
sources: Кононов Н. В. Код Дурова. Реальная история «ВКонтакте» и её создателя. М.: Манн, Иванов и Фербер, 2012.

rendering.ja: ゲーム『アルファ・ロメオ』

«Альфа-ромео».rationale: Preserves the denotation and clear identification of the referent as a game title rather than the automobile brand, integrating the clarifying noun smoothly into running text without clunky parenthetical glosses.

Добрая машина пропаганды.finding: Alexey Navalny's decentralized agitation project, first proposed at a Moscow opposition rally on 5 March 2012 and launched via the site Mashina.org on 29 May 2012. The name was deliberately self-ironic: Navalny framed it as the 'kind/good' counterweight to the state's 'evil' propaganda machine (TV and pro-Kremlin media), reclaiming the negatively loaded word 'propaganda' rather than denying that his side also agitated. It was soon renamed 'Добрая машина правды' (Good Machine of Truth), and by 2013 the project had effectively folded. For a 2013 Russian reader the name signalled Navalny's brand of sarcastic, meme-aware political branding.

rendering.ja: 「善良なるプロパガンダ・マシン」

Добрая машина пропаганды.rationale: All three renderings keep the literal, oxymoronic name as a quoted title so the irony of calling one's own side a 'propaganda machine' survives; what is sacrificed is the untranslatable resonance with Navalny's own polemical term 'propaganda machine' for state TV, which surrounding narrative context must supply. Japanese uses the slightly literary 善良なる to keep the mock-heroic register suitable for a serious business biography.

Дуров-старший.finding: Дуров-старший in the 2013 press context denotes Nikolai Valeryevich Durov (b. 1980), Pavel's brother four years his senior — a three-time IMO gold medalist, two-time PhD (St. Petersburg and Bonn, under Faltings), Steklov Institute researcher, and VKontakte's technical director from 2006. The Russian suffix -старший is a press device distinguishing two prominent brothers of the same surname, not a reference to their father Valery Durov, a philology classicist who was never publicly prominent in the VK story. For a 2013 Russian reader it carried the connotation of the reclusive mathematical genius behind the popular site that the flamboyant Pavel fronted.

rendering.ja: 兄のニコライ・ドゥーロフ

Дуров-старший.rationale: In all three languages the bare '-старший' pattern ('the elder Durov', 大杜罗夫) is read as the father, so I gave up the compact surname-only form and made the kinship plus first name explicit, preserving denotation and the serious-biography register; the slight loss is the original's terse journalistic shorthand.

«ВКонтакте».finding: ВКонтакте is the Russian social network Pavel Durov co-founded with his brother Nikolai in 2006; its name literally means 'In Contact'. Around 2013 it was Russia's dominant social platform (monthly reach ~84% of Runet), culturally the Facebook of the Russian-speaking world, and the site of Durov's public persona. The company rebranded to 'VK' in 2017, so readers today often know the brand simply as VK.

rendering.zh: VKontakte（俄罗斯社交网络“接触网”）
rendering.ja: VKontakte（ヴコンタクテ、ロシアのSNS）

«ВКонтакте».rationale: Keep the brand name 'VKontakte' unchanged in all three languages for book-wide consistency, as the existing English, Japanese and Chinese Wikipedia editions do; sacrifice the Russian pun 'in contact' but recover it once with a brief gloss at first mention in zh and ja, where readers have no organic memory of the 2000s Russian web. Denotation and register (neutral brand name) are preserved; the wordplay is conceded.

Дуров.finding: Surname of Pavel Valeryevich Durov (Павел Валерьевич Дуров, b. 1984), St. Petersburg-born founder of VKontakte; in a 2013 Russian press biography it is the unmarked family name of the central subject, already widely known to Russian internet users as the face of VK. English media and Wikipedia use the scholarly Latinization Durov (not Duroff). Japanese Wikipedia standardizes ドゥーロフ with long ウー. Chinese coverage splits 杜洛夫 (zh.wikipedia title) and 杜罗夫 (mainland press); the latter matches prior book segments.
Дуров.rationale: Preserved denotation and book-wide consistency of the family name; sacrificed zh.wikipedia’s 杜洛夫 in favour of the already-chosen 杜罗夫 so Chinese chapters do not split the same person.

ВКонтакте.finding: Russia's dominant social network, founded in 2006 by Pavel Durov and his brother Nikolai, modeled initially on Facebook. By 2013 it was the default internet platform for Russian-speaking youth — the 'Russian Facebook' — with its reputation slightly raffish (pirated music, meme pages, political protest) and its brand inseparable from Durov himself. The name literally means 'in touch / in contact'. It was commonly shortened to 'VK' colloquially even then; the official corporate rebrand to VK came only in 2014–2021.
ВКонтакте.rationale: Denotation and the brand's period register are preserved by keeping the proper noun; Japanese gets the established katakana form フコンタクテ used by ja.wikipedia and Japanese business media, while Chinese and English keep the Latin-script name already standard in those Wikipedias. The zh gloss sacrifices brevity to supply the 'Russian Facebook' cultural analogue that a Chinese reader needs; the parenthetical VK anticipates the colloquial shortening used throughout the book.

Алексей Навальный.finding: Alexei Navalny (1976–2024) was a Russian lawyer and anti-corruption activist who rose to prominence through his blog investigations into state corruption and projects like Rospil and the 'Good Machine of Propaganda' (Добрая машина правды). By 2011–2012 he had become the most visible leader of the protest movement against alleged election fraud and Putin's return to the presidency; for a Russian reader in 2013 his name immediately signified internet-native opposition politics and a direct challenge to the Kremlin. He later ran for Moscow mayor (2013, 27% of the vote), was repeatedly imprisoned, and died in a penal colony in February 2024.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/アレクセイ・ナワリヌイ

rendering.ja: アレクセイ・ナワリヌイ

Алексей Навальный.rationale: All three renderings are the established standard transliterations in their respective Wikipedias and major media. Denotation (the person's identity) is fully preserved in each; connotation (his role as opposition leader) must be supplied by surrounding context in the biography text rather than by the name itself. Register is formal and appropriate for a serious biography in all three languages.

Лев и Слава.finding: Refers to Lev Leviev (Лев Левиев, b. 1984) and Vyacheslav Mirilashvili (Вячеслав Мирилашвили, b. 1984), the two Israeli-Russian investors who co-founded VKontakte with Pavel Durov in 2006. 'Слава' is the standard Russian diminutive of Вячеслав, and the pairing 'Лев и Слава' mirrors the informal, startup-culture register common in Russian tech journalism of the early 2010s, treating these young co-founders as peers rather than formal business figures. The English Wikipedia uses 'Lev Leviev' and 'Vyacheslav Mirilashvili' as full names; the Russian Wikipedia itself uses 'Лев и Вячеслав' in one passage, confirming that even encyclopedic Russian prose oscillates between informal and formal first-name usage for these figures.
Лев и Слава.rationale: All three renderings preserve both denotation (correct individuals) and the informal register of the source by keeping first names / diminutives rather than expanding to full names. The slight loss is the specifically Russian cultural warmth of the diminutive 'Слава', which has no exact equivalent in any target language, but 'Slava' / '斯拉瓦' / 'スラヴァ' are the established short forms in each language and carry the same informal feel.

Гришин.finding: Гришин is Dmitry Sergeevich Grishin (Дмитрий Сергеевич Гришин, b. 1978), who in 2013 was CEO and chairman of the board of Mail.ru Group and a key figure in the corporate battle over VKontakte. He succeeded Yuri Milner as CEO in April 2003 and as chairman in 2012; under him Mail.ru Group accumulated a 39.99% stake in VKontakte by 2011 and he publicly voiced the company's intentions toward the social network, making him the natural recipient of a game developer's complaint in the Durov saga. A Russian business reader would instantly recognize Grishin as the operational head of Mail.ru distinct from Milner, whom he succeeded twice at the top of the holding. The confusion on the part of translators between Grishin and Milner is understandable because they shared the CEO and chairman roles over the years, but by 2013 Grishin was the active CEO-chairman and Milner had moved on.
Гришин.rationale: Denotation (the correct person and his Mail.ru role) is fully preserved in all three languages; the established Chinese Wikipedia form 格里申 and the standard Japanese surname transcription グリシン both carry the name faithfully, while the brief surname form matches the source's bare-name usage. What is sacrificed is disambiguation: the rendering alone cannot tell a reader it is Dmitry, not another Grishin, though context should supply that.

«Одноклассники».finding: Odnoklassniki (ok.ru) is a Russian social network launched in 2006, explicitly modeled on Classmates.com, focused on reconnecting former schoolmates and classmates. Around 2013 it was one of the top Russian social networks alongside VKontakte, but had a somewhat older, more mass-market/provincial user demographic compared to VK's younger, urban audience — a connotation Russian readers would pick up on. It is a brand name, not the generic word 'classmates', though the name itself is transparent to Russian speakers.

rendering.ja: オドノクラースニキ(Odnoklassniki、Classmates.comのロシア版)

«Одноклассники».rationale: Preserved the proper-name denotation (brand, not generic 'classmates') while adding a brief gloss tying it to the internationally known Classmates.com model, sacrificing full brevity for clarity; register kept neutral/informational as befits a business biography.

Невского.finding: Nevsky Prospect (Невский проспект) is the principal avenue of Saint Petersburg, running 4.5 km from the Admiralty to the Alexander Nevsky Lavra. It is the city's main commercial and cultural artery, a UNESCO World Heritage component, and a universal Russian shorthand for peak urban foot traffic. In the 2013 Durov biography it serves as a crowd-density comparator, instantly legible to any Russian reader as 'the busiest, most iconic street imaginable.' The English convention retains the transliteration 'Prospekt' rather than translating it as 'Avenue'; Chinese uses 涅瓦大街 (the short form preferred on zh-wiki); Japanese uses ネフスキー大通り, translating проспект as 大通り.
Невского.rationale: All three renderings preserve denotation and connotation (the iconic, busiest street in Petersburg) while matching the established convention in each target-language Wikipedia and press. The English form sacrifices naturalness ('Prospekt' is opaque to monolingual readers) but gains precision and matches universal English-language usage; the Chinese and Japanese forms sacrifice the foreign flavor of проспект by translating it, which is the norm in those languages.

Лев Левиев.finding: Lev Binzumovich Leviev (born 1984) is a Russian-Israeli entrepreneur and investor who co-founded VKontakte in 2006 with Vyacheslav Mirilashvili and Pavel Durov, also co-founding the major data center operator Selectel. For Russian readers in 2013, he was a key figure in the VK equity drama involving Mail.ru and UCP, distinct from but frequently confusingly sharing a name with the older diamond oligarch Lev Avnerovich Leviev.
Лев Левиев.rationale: Preserved the standard orthographic and phonetic transliteration of the proper name across all three target languages; sacrificed immediate disambiguation from the diamond magnate in the name string itself, relying on narrative context to clarify his identity.

Алишер Усманов.finding: Alisher Burkhanovich Usmanov is an Uzbek-born Russian oligarch, founded USM Holdings (Metalloinvest, MegaFon) and owned Kommersant; through DST and Mail.ru Group he co-invested with Yuri Milner in Facebook, VKontakte and other tech assets. Around 2013 he was repeatedly ranked as Russia's richest man by Forbes and was widely seen as close to the Kremlin and personally to Putin, so 'по просьбе власти' fits the image of an oligarch whose business moves could be enacted at official request. For a 2013 Russian reader he connoted the interconnected world of state-aligned billionaire capital, not just 'a tech investor'.

rendering.ja: アリシェル・ウスマノフ

Алишер Усманов.rationale: Keeps denotation in all three: the established transliteration of the name an educated reader would already recognize from Forbes rankings and, in en/zh/ja media, coverage of his tech and sports dealings. The embedded connotation of 'Kremlin-aligned oligarch' is sacrificed as a bare name carries none of it, and the register stays neutral as befits a reported biography.

Кузя.finding: In Nikolay Kononov's 2013 book 'The Durov Code' (Код Дурова), 'Кузя' (Kuzya) is the internal team nickname for early VKontakte developer/engineer Mikhail Kuznetsov (Михаил Кузнецов). Diminutive hypocorisms formed with '-я' from surnames (Kuznetsov -> Kuzya) are common informal shorthand in Russian male tech and university circles, blending collegiality and insider culture without pejorative tone.
sources: Кононов Н. В. Код Дурова. Реальная история «ВКонтакте» и её создателя. — М.: Манн, Иванов и Фербер, 2012.
Кузя.rationale: Preserved the informal intra-team nickname verbatim in standard phonetic transliteration across all three target languages to maintain the insider startup ambiance of the original dialogue and narrative, sacrificing immediate explicit surname recognition (Kuznetsov) which can be clarified by apposition or context if needed.

«Мегафон».finding: MegaFon is one of Russia's 'big three' mobile network operators (alongside MTS and Beeline), founded in 1993 as North-West GSM and rebranded MegaFon in 2002. In a 2013 Durov/VKontakte biography, it would be mentioned as a familiar, everyday nationwide telecom brand — the kind of company any Russian reader instantly recognizes, comparable to Verizon/AT&T in the US context, with no special irony or subculture connotation, just standard corporate/business register.

rendering.ja: メガフォン（ロシアの携帯通信事業者）

«Мегафон».rationale: Preserve the official Latin-brand denotation (MegaFon) as already used by English readers; for zh/ja keep a short parenthetical gloss since the brand isn't otherwise known, sacrificing brevity for clarity while keeping neutral business register intact.

Гриз.finding: The term appears to be a nickname or surname of a teacher/tutor at the gifted school Pavel Durov attended after returning from Italy, as described in Nikolai Kononov's 2013 biography 'Код Дурова'. The Wikipedia article on the book confirms Durov attended a 'strong school for gifted children' but does not name individual teachers. No independent Wikipedia article or other easily verifiable source identifies a person called 'Гриз' in connection with Durov's schooling. The name likely functions as a familiar nickname (possibly from a surname or a characteristic), carrying the informal register of school-community reference. Without further access to the book text or additional sources, the exact identity and full name remain unconfirmed.
Гриз.rationale: All three renderings preserve denotation by transliterating the nickname as-is, which is the safest approach for an unverified personal name that may reappear later in the text. Connotation (informal school nickname) is partially lost since the target-language reader cannot tell it is a nickname rather than a surname, but inventing an explanation would risk inaccuracy.

МГУ.finding: МГУ is the everyday Russian abbreviation of Московский государственный университет имени М. В. Ломоносова (Lomonosov Moscow State University), Russia’s oldest and most prestigious comprehensive university, founded in 1755. For a 2013 Russian reader it names the country’s flagship academic brand, not a generic Moscow campus: admission and faculty there still signal elite status. English, Chinese and Japanese Wikipedia already treat it as that named institution rather than a opaque initialism.
МГУ.rationale: Expanded the opaque abbreviation to each language’s established short name so denotation and prestige register survive; dropped the Lomonosov eponym and Cyrillic МГУ, which would be noise in a biography for non-Russian readers.

Бертова.finding: Бертова returns no Wikipedia article in Russian, and the Russian Wikipedia article on the book «Код Дурова» does not mention her. She appears to be a minor real-life acquaintance from the Durov family's past, not a public figure; the surname is an ordinary Russian feminine form (Бертов), and for a 2013 Russian reader it carried no fixed public referent. The comedy in the scene comes from the formal «Анна Дмитриевна» address, not from any famous associations.
Бертова.rationale: Preserves denotation (the proper name) through conventional target-language transliteration in each language; sacrifices any connotation because none is documented. Chinese uses the standard Russian surname pattern -ova → 娃; Japanese uses the natural Russian -ova → ワ rather than a hypercorrect ヴァ.

Мильнер.finding: Юрий Борисович (Бенционович) Мильнер, born 11 Nov 1961 in Moscow, theoretical-physics graduate of MSU, Wharton-educated, ex-Menatep investment executive; in 2005 founded Digital Sky Technologies (later DST Global). In 2007 DST bought 24.99% of VKontakte from existing shareholders for $16.3m — the deal that made him the counterparty figure in the Durov VK story. By 2013 a Russian reader knew him as the 'global' investor whose DST had bought into Facebook, Zynga, Twitter and Groupon, co-owner of Mail.ru Group; son of economist Bentsion Milner, Israeli citizen since 1999.
Мильнер.rationale: Keeps denotation exactly (Yuri Milner of DST, buyer of ~24.99% of VK in 2007) and the neutral-formal register of business biography; the standard transliterations are each audience's established form (zh uses 尤里·米尔纳 in simplified, ja uses ユーリ・ミルナー per the Japanese Wikipedia title). The DST/VK context should be supplied by the surrounding segment rather than the name itself; given-name retention keeps him distinct from any other 'Milner' and from Durov. Chinese rendering: use 尤里·米尔纳 at first mention with DST (数字天空技术) nearby so the reader places him without a footnote.

Влад.finding: Влад is Vladislav ('Vlad') Tsyplukhin (Владислав Цыплухин), who around 2013 was the head of VKontakte's press service / communications, frequently the company's public voice in disputes (e.g. statements on copyright and on Durov's 2011 Victory Day post). Russian Wikipedia's articles on VKontakte and Durov cite him as 'руководитель пресс-службы Владислав Цыплухин'; he later co-founded the Komitet publishing house (vc.ru, TJournal) and was product director at Coub. The bare diminutive 'Влад' in the biography signals Durov's inner-circle informality, but the referent is identifiable as Tsyplukhin, the VK PR chief.

rendering.en: Vlad (Vladislav Tsyplukhin, VK's head of press relations)
rendering.zh: 弗拉德（即VK新闻负责人弗拉季斯拉夫·齐普卢欣）
rendering.ja: ヴラド（VK広報担当のウラディスラフ・ツィプルーヒン）

Влад.rationale: The rendering keeps the familiar first-name form 'Vlad' (preserving the informal in-group register Durov used) while a bracketed identification of Tsyplukhin, the press-service head, gives readers the denotation that Russian-context readers would infer from context. Transliterations follow the standard systems for each language; the gloss is sacrificed to a brief apposition since a bare 'Влад' alone is opaque outside Russia.

Голден Телеком.finding: Golden Telecom was a major Russian/CIS telecommunications and internet backbone provider founded in the 1990s (originally as Sovintel/Golden Telecom Inc., US-registered), providing corporate internet, data transit and telephony services across Russia and the CIS. It was acquired by VimpelCom (Beeline) in 2008, becoming a well-known example of a large Western-style telecom operator that had built key internet infrastructure in Russia. For a Russian reader circa 2013, the name evokes a serious, established corporate telecom brand of the 2000s rather than any internet-culture slang.

rendering.ja: ゴールデン・テレコム

Голден Телеком.rationale: Preserved the original English corporate name (denotation and register) since it was itself an English-named company operating in Russia; sacrificed any connotative texture since the name carried none beyond corporate prestige. For zh, kept the English name parenthetically since 'Golden Telecom' as transliterated is not widely fixed in Chinese sources, prioritizing clarity over a fully naturalized Chinese name.

Мирилашвили.finding: Это фамилия Вячеслава Михайловича Мирилашвили, однокурсника Павла Дурова, соучредителя и первоначально крупнейшего акционера «ВКонтакте». Для российского читателя около 2013 года она обозначала не просто участника стартапа, а обеспеченного инвестора, предоставившего проекту доступ к капиталу своей семьи; сама фамилия употреблялась нейтрально, без прозвищной или иронической окраски. В современных англоязычных источниках он также известен как Yitzchak Mirilashvili, однако в повествовании о российском периоде уместно сохранять форму Vyacheslav и устоявшееся написание фамилии Mirilashvili.
Мирилашвили.rationale: Сохранены денотат, нейтральный биографический регистр и узнаваемая грузинская структура фамилии; культурный намек на грузино-еврейское происхождение и нынешнее имя Yitzchak не поясняются, поскольку в исходном употреблении фамилия сама по себе их не актуализирует.

Министерство образования.finding: In a 2013 Russian text this refers to the Russian federal ministry formally called Министерство образования и науки Российской Федерации (Минобрнауки, Ministry of Education and Science, 2004–2018). Journalistic and colloquial usage routinely shortened it to «Министерство образования». For a Russian reader it denoted the state authority over schools and universities — the bureaucratic establishment that figures like Durov chafed against; the country's name needed no qualifier in Russian. In English, Chinese or Japanese, however, 'Ministry of Education' without a country qualifier is ambiguous (Japan has 文部科学省, China has its own 教育部), so the qualifier must be added.
Министерство образования.rationale: Preserves denotation (the specific federal ministry) and neutral register; adds an explicit country qualifier in all three target languages to remove ambiguity for non-Russian readers. Sacrifices the literal full official name ('and Science'), matching the source text's own shortening and keeping the prose natural.

Левиев.finding: Refers to Lev Avnerovich Leviev (born 1984), co-founder of VKontakte alongside Vyacheslav Mirilashvili and Pavel Durov. In Durov's biography, he is a central character representing the financial and strategic co-founding bloc, and is distinct from the diamond oligarch Lev Avnerovich Leviev (Leviev/Levayev, born 1956). In Russian media and inside VKontakte lore, he is universally referred to simply as Leviev, forming with Mirilashvili the duo that provided VK's initial seed capital and server infrastructure.
Левиев.rationale: Preserves standard biographical transliteration and neutral journalistic register across EN, ZH, and JA; gives up explicit disambiguation in the running text (such as adding first names or patronymics) to match Russian source usage where context makes his role obvious.

Одноклассники.finding: «Одноклассники» refers to the Russian social network launched in 2006 by Albert Popkov, built around reconnecting with former classmates and acquaintances. By 2013 it was a mass-market platform with more than 200 million registered accounts and a major competitor to VKontakte, though VKontakte had overtaken it in popularity by late 2008. For Russian readers, the name functioned unmistakably as a brand while still transparently meaning “classmates,” evoking school ties and reunion-style social networking.
Одноклассники.rationale: The English and Japanese forms preserve the established brand identity but give up the Russian name’s immediately transparent meaning. The Chinese form keeps the internationally recognizable brand and adds the concise analogue “同学网,” preserving its classmate-reconnection connotation without a footnote.

Михаил Мирилашвили.finding: Это Михаил Михайлович Мирилашвили (род. 1960), отец Вячеслава («Славы») Мирилашвили, петербургский предприниматель, связанный с холдингом «ПетроМир», игорным бизнесом и семьёй сооснователей «ВКонтакте». В 2003 году его приговорили к 12 годам заключения по делу о похищении людей, похитивших его отца — Михаила Габриэловича Мирилашвили; таким образом, упоминаемый «дед» — другой Михаил Мирилашвили. Для российского читателя 2013 года имя несло ассоциации с богатством, петербургским игорным бизнесом, влиятельностью и громким уголовным делом.

rendering.zh: 米哈伊尔·米哈伊洛维奇·米里拉什维利
rendering.ja: ミハイル・ミハイロヴィチ・ミリラシヴィリ

Михаил Мирилашвили.rationale: Полное имя с отчеством сохраняет денотацию и устраняет смешение с отцом героя уголовного дела, Михаилом Габриэловичем. Оно несколько повышает формальность по сравнению с исходным кратким именем, но не добавляет оценочной или криминальной окраски, которую должен передавать контекст.

День города.finding: День города is the annual civic festival each Russian city holds to mark its founding, typically with concerts, street fairs and fireworks on a weekend near the anniversary date. In the Durov/VKontakte biography it refers to St. Petersburg's City Day, tied to the city's founding on 27 May 1703 (Peter and Paul Fortress), which places the episode in late May in St. Petersburg. For a 2013 Russian reader it connotes a familiar, festive, mass street holiday — not an official state event — and primarily functions as a time-and-place marker in the narrative.

rendering.en: the city's founding-day festival (City Day, late May)
rendering.zh: 建城节（圣彼得堡城市日，五月底）
rendering.ja: 市の記念日（サンクトペテルブルク建都祭、5月末）

День города.rationale: All three preserve the denotation (annual founding-anniversary celebration) and explicitly restore the late-May timing cue the original carries implicitly; the light parenthetical costs a little narrative flow but saves the chronological signal, sacrificing only the effortless familiarity Russian readers have with the bare term.

Wired.finding: Wired is a US technology and culture magazine founded in San Francisco in 1993, published by Condé Nast, covering the impact of emerging technologies on culture, economy, and politics. In the Russian Wikipedia article it is referred to simply as 'Wired' in Latin script without a translated name. By 2013, a Wired journalist visiting VKontakte would have carried the connotation of mainstream Western tech-media validation of a Russian startup. The magazine had a Japanese edition (WIRED日本版) running from 1994–1998 and relaunched in 2011, so Japanese readers in 2013 knew it well. In Chinese, the established rendering is 《连线》杂志.
Wired.rationale: English keeps the bare name as the magazine styles itself. Chinese uses the established translated title 《连线》 with the classifier 杂志 for clarity, preserving denotation and register. Japanese uses 『WIRED』誌 in all-caps Latin as the Japanese edition itself does, preserving the brand identity that Japanese readers recognize; the 誌 suffix disambiguates it as a publication rather than a person or concept. In all three languages, connotation of Western tech-media prestige is carried implicitly by the name itself.
